Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2026-03-28 09:00 PT
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Taylor Nguyen (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (SE), Omar Li (Solutions), Mark Rivers (CTO - BrightHealth), Sana Patel (Sr ML Eng), Luis Gomez (Platform Eng)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Taylor gave a walkthrough of Redwood's Hosted API for chat/text generation focusing on streaming, generation params (temp, top_p, max_tokens), and retry/failover patterns. Priya demoed a live example showing streaming partial tokens and a fallback to a smaller model when latency spiked. Customer raised questions about data residency, SOC2/KMS, and how token costs are measured; next steps were to run a 2-week pilot and exchange security docs and benchmarking scripts.

Topics:
- Streaming response behavior and partial tokens
- Generation params and quality vs cost tradeoffs
- Retry/backoff and model failover strategies
- Prefix/KV caching, batching, and cost controls
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, VPC options

Action items (from call):
- See metadata action_items above for owners/due dates.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, occasional transcription artifacts present):
[00:00] Taylor: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Taylor, I look after strategic accounts. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer, and Omar from solutions.
[00:14] Mark: Hey, Mark here. Thanks, Taylor. We're hoping to understand how Redwood's hosted API would fit into our chat assistant — mostly worried about latency and token costs.
[00:24] Taylor: Totally, that's the right place to start. Priya will demo streaming and show how parameters affect latency/cost, then we'll cover retries and fallback patterns.
[00:33] Priya: Hi all. I'll share my screen — let me know if you don't see the repo. (screen noise) Okay, pull up a basic chat example. We're using the hosted chat endpoint, streaming on, so you get chunks as the model emits.
[00:50] Sana: Quick Q — does streaming mean we pay per chunk? We bill per token, right?
[00:56] Priya: Good question. Billing is per token generated/consumed. Streaming just changes how the bytes arrive; cost is driven by tokens and model size. But it also affects perceived latency because you can render partial tokens faster.
[01:12] Luis: If we enable streaming, what's the impact on our frontend websocket connections and reconnect logic?
[01:19] Omar: In our experience, keep an eye on connection timeouts and use backpressure controls. Redwood exposes a stream checkpoint so you can resume in some cases, but we recommended graceful reconnects.
[01:33] Mark: Can you demo parameter tuning? We have a strict 400ms latency target for short replies.
[01:40] Priya: Sure. So temperature, top_p, and max_tokens are the main knobs. For tight latency like 400ms, we usually reduce max_tokens, pick a smaller model family for short turns, and enable prefix caching for repeated prompts.
[01:54] (screen showing code)
[01:57] Priya: Example: model=gpt-neo-lite (note: placeholder), max_tokens=40, temperature=0.2, stream=true. You can see partial chunks arriving.
[02:08] (audio: typing)
[02:10] Taylor: Remember there are also batching and autoscaling layers on the server — if you need high throughput we tune batching window to balance latency/cost.
[02:22] Sana: About caching — you mentioned prefix caching and KV cache earlier. Are those automatic?
[02:29] Priya: Redwood has automatic prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts — it's workload-dependent. For a chat assistant with consistent system prompt + few-shot examples, you can cache the KV and save tokens per request. But there are TTLs and cache invalidation rules — we'll share doc.
[02:44] Luis: What about retry patterns? If the model times out or we get 5xx — what's recommended?
[02:50] Priya: We recommend exponential backoff with jitter, and a policy of fallback to a compatible cheaper/fast model after N retries. For example, try the primary model with 2 quick retries, if still failing, route to a smaller distil variant, and flag for async recompute if quality matters.
[03:06] Mark: How do we preserve conversation state if we fallback to a smaller model? We worry about hallucination risks.
[03:12] Priya: Great point. Options: keep response labeled as 'degraded' in the UI, run a background job to re-run on the higher-quality model and patch if necessary, or only fallback for non-critical messages. We log the fallback event with trace ids so you can reconcile.
[03:28] (brief crosstalk)
[03:35] Sana: Can you show an actual failure scenario?
[03:38] Priya: Yes — I'll throttle the primary model to simulate latency spike. (typing) You should see the streaming stall, then the router kicks in and switches to the smaller model after the timeout threshold.
[03:53] (audio artifact)
[03:55] Priya: And streaming resumes with the smaller model — note the token pattern and slightly simpler phrasing.
[04:05] Mark: That makes sense. For audit we need a record of which model served which request. Is that in the logs?
[04:11] Taylor: Yes — per-request metadata includes model_id, latency, tokens_in/out, route decision, and a trace id. We can surface that in the console and export to S3.
[04:22] Luis: What about data retention and encryption — we're in healthcare so SOC 2 and KMS are must-haves.
[04:29] Taylor: We support SOC 2 (Type II), customer-managed KMS for Private deployments, and Hosted customers can use Redwood's managed keys with strict controls. For VPC/private, we support VPC peering and on-prem options. We'll send the compliance pack after the call.
[04:45] Sana: If we go hosted, are there tenancy options? We need to ensure no co-mingling of sensitive embeddings for inference.
[04:52] Omar: For sensitive workloads, Dedicated or Private is recommended — Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and isolation; Private gives you complete control. Hosted has strict isolation at the tenant level but not a dedicated GPU pool unless you buy Dedicated.
[05:07] Mark: Cost — can you give a rough ballpark? We want to compare served tokens at 100k/month.
[05:13] Taylor: I'll send a pricing sheet, but rough order: larger models are 3-5x the token cost of smaller variants. The Optimize tool can recommend quantization and batching that often reduces unit cost by 30-60% depending on sequence length.
[05:31] Sana: On quantization — do you support int8 or 4-bit flows in hosted?
[05:36] Priya: Hosted supports quantized variants we ship — often 8-bit fast kernels. For extreme density we recommend Private where you can run custom quantized kernels. We also do kernel selection automatically based on model and sequence length.
[05:50] Mark: How do we measure quality regressions when swapping quantized/fallback models?
[05:55] Priya: Redwood Optimize ties quality checks to eval sets and can alert on regression thresholds, plus you can pin model versions and do canary rollouts.
[06:05] (pause)
[06:12] Priya: Quick demo of console: you can see per-route dashboards, token breakdown, per-model latency percentiles, and a replay for failing requests.
[06:23] (screen share showing console)
[06:30] Luis: Can we integrate with our PagerDuty if latency SLOs breach?
[06:33] Taylor: Yep — console supports webhooks and alert integrations (PagerDuty, Slack).
[06:38] Mark: For the POC we'll need a small benchmark run — can you provide a script?
[06:43] Priya: We'll send a lightweight benchmark harness with curl/node examples and a load config. It will measure p50/p95 latency and token throughput.
[06:51] Sana: We want results that reflect our prompts — I'll paste a short prompt set.
[06:56] Mark: On rollout, we prefer canary by user cohort. Does Redwood support that?
[07:01] Omar: Yes — you can route by header/identity, split traffic, and have automatic fallback policies. We'll share an example config.
[07:09] (noise)
[07:12] Priya: Now a quick look at retry/backoff code snippet — here's pseudo: try request, on 5xx do exponential backoff with jitter, after two retries perform model-switch to 'fast-small' and tag response. There was a small typo in the earlier doc where 'retry' was misspelled as 'retire' in the sample.
[07:33] Sana: (laughs) That's the one-liner that got us in trouble.
[07:38] Mark: What about partial tokens arriving — do we need to reassemble on mobile?
[07:44] Priya: We send complete token deltas. On mobile, you render chunks as they arrive. If you need guaranteed sentence boundaries, do a small buffering on the client for smoother UX.
[07:57] Luis: Any tricks to reduce tokens without harming quality?
[08:01] Priya: Several: compress context by removing redundant system messages, use embeddings for retrieval then only send top-K excerpts, and canonicalize user queries. Also use short prompting patterns and role separation to keep few-shot examples minimal.
[08:18] Mark: Does Redwood support function/tool calling or structured outputs?
[08:22] Priya: Yes — hosted chat supports structured output and function calling. We can also return JSON schemas to help downstream parsing.
[08:30] (brief pause)
[08:34] Sana: Security follow-up — we need an answer on RBAC for the console and audit log retention.
[08:40] Taylor: RBAC with SSO (SAML/OIDC) is supported and audit logs can be retained for configurable windows; for enterprise you can push logs to your SIEM. We'll include retention options in the security pack.
[08:54] Mark: Regarding latency guarantees — what SLAs exist for hosted?
[08:59] Taylor: Hosted tier has best-effort latency targets; Dedicated and Private have SLA-backed targets. If you require 99.9 latency SLOs, Dedicated is the recommendation.
[09:12] Luis: For the pilot we prefer hosted first and then expand to Dedicated if we need guaranteed latency. Does that path make sense?
[09:18] Omar: That's common — start hosted to iterate on prompts and flows, then migrate to Dedicated when throughput needs or compliance require it.
[09:27] Mark: OK. Can we talk about observability? We want per-request token costs surfaced to product metrics.
[09:33] Priya: Console exposes token_in/out and cost estimates per request. You can tag routes to map to product features and roll up cost.
[09:43] Sana: Any gotchas on streaming with mobile networks?
[09:47] Priya: On flaky networks, fallbacks and idempotency keys matter. We recommend use of incremental checkpoints and a client-side retry policy tied to idempotency keys so duplicate responses can be detected.
[09:59] (short silence)
[10:05] Mark: About model naming — I'm seeing a few different labels, what's the safe pattern?
[10:09] Priya: We publish a model catalog with versioned names. For example 'rw-chat-v1.3' and quantized variants like 'rw-chat-v1.3-8q'. Avoid hardcoding internal model flavors; pin to stable version ids.
[10:23] Luis: Do you support embedding the KV cache by customer so they don't cross-tenant?
[10:29] Taylor: Caches are tenant-scoped; for Dedicated/Private you get physical isolation. For hosted, tenant-level logical isolation is applied.
[10:38] Sana: One more question — what about realtime moderation/filters?
[10:42] Priya: We have a content safety pipeline that can run pre- or post-generation policies. You can opt into blocking or tagging responses. Latency tradeoffs exist if you run synchronous checks; you can also do async audits.
[10:58] (crosstalk)
[11:05] Mark: This has been useful. Let's recap next steps.
[11:09] Taylor: Recap: we'll send pricing, SOC2/security pack, benchmark harness, and a sample canary config. Customer to share prompt set and confirm pilot date.
[11:19] Mark: Sounds good. We'll aim to confirm the POC start by Friday.
[11:23] Sana: I'll get the prompt set over by Tuesday.
[11:26] Luis: I'll loop in infra for the networking review.
[11:29] Taylor: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with artifacts.
[11:34] (meeting closes)
